name: caveat-passes-fix-the-weak-phrase
description: A self-correction pass tends to fix the hedged phrasing it was thinking about and leave the stronger false claim standing nearby

When you write a caveat admitting a limitation, you correct the phrasing that was
on your mind — and the stronger, more clearly false claim two lines away survives,
now *endorsed* by sitting next to an apparently thorough admission.

Measured in AJC `RiemannRoch/Ledger/VanishingFieldDescent.lean` (run 0074 r7). A
commit whose entire purpose was admitting a producer had no exhibited instance
downgraded "the first `UniformVanishing` instance" to "the first producer" — and

theorem carries an explicit hypothesis, so "unconditional" was the flatly false
word, and it was the one the caveat pass missed. Found by fresh-context review,
not by the pass that wrote the caveat.

**Why:** self-correction is anchored on the sentence that prompted it. The reader
who stops at the earlier, stronger claim gets the opposite of what the caveat
intended, and the caveat's presence makes the page *look* audited.

**How to apply:** after writing any caveat or retraction, grep the file — and the
whole project — for the *strongest* form of the claim being weakened, not the form
you just edited. Search for absolute adjectives specifically: "unconditional",
"complete", "closed", "always", "any". Then check whether each still survives its
own caveat. Same discipline as grepping a withdrawn claim's text rather than the
file you edited; the retraction and the claim are rarely in the same place.

[[absence-claims-need-the-whole-project]], [[subsingleton-not-finrank-for-vanishing]].
